summary: Comments from UCLA-NMC on the draft Data Transfer Protocol and File Transfer Protocol after trying to implement them. They point out an ambiguity in the length of the sequence number field and suggest simplifying the transaction header, and raise other problems the implementation revealed.

plainLanguage.summary: UCLA-NMC reports two problems it found while trying to implement proposed data and file transfer protocols. One concerns inconsistent sequence-number sizes; the other concerns how Append identifies a file's end.

questions: what ambiguity did ucla find in sequence numbers
subtitle: UCLA-NMC identifies ambiguities found while implementing draft transfer protocols.

tldr.problem: Implementation attempts exposed ambiguities in the proposed Data Transfer and File Transfer Protocols.
tldr.mechanism: UCLA-NMC discusses inconsistent sequence-number sizes and unclear meaning for the Append transaction.
tldr.outcome: The author argues that resolving these questions would help accelerate implementation at UCLA-NMC.

today: RFC 250 is implementation feedback on proposed transfer protocols published in October 1971. The unit metadata lists its status as Unknown.

sections.title: Implementation Experience
sections.content: UCLA-NMC had attempted to implement the proposed Data Transfer Protocol and File Transfer Protocol as interest grew in transferring more data than typical Telnet exchanges. The work revealed issues that the RFC asks protocol designers to clarify.
sections.plainLanguage: UCLA-NMC tried to build the proposed transfer protocols and found unclear points. This RFC shares those implementation observations.

sections.title: Sequence Number Size
sections.content: The RFC says RFC 171 describes a 16-bit sequence-number field in a descriptor and count transaction but provides only 8 bits in the error-codes transaction. The author considers 8 bits sufficient and suggests removing two NUL bytes from the descriptor and count header, reducing it to 48 bits.
sections.plainLanguage: Different transactions use different sizes for the sequence number. The author suggests using 8 bits and removing two NUL bytes to make the header smaller.

sections.title: Meaning of Append
sections.content:
At UCLA's SEX timesharing system, the program reading a file determines when it has reached the file's end. The author says this makes the meaning of Append unclear, particularly because the proposed Mail Box Protocol uses the Append feature.

The RFC argues that resolving these ambiguities could accelerate implementation at UCLA-NMC.
sections.plainLanguage: The system may let a reading program decide when a file ends, which leaves Append unclear. The author says this matters because the mailbox proposal relies on Append.
